chunks: "Microarchitecture is how a processor actually implements its instruction set. The ISA says what instructions exist, what the registers are and what each instruction means.

The microarchitecture is the internal design that makes those instructions happen: how many pipeline stages, whether it executes in order or out of order, how many instructions it issues per cycle, what the caches look like, what branch predictor it uses, how wide the buses are.
The key idea is that one ISA can have many microarchitectures.

Arm's Cortex-A53 and Cortex-A76 both run the same ARMv8-A software, but the A53 is a small in-order core and the A76 is a big out-of-order one, so the A76 is much faster and bigger and uses more power.
Intel and AMD both implement x86-64 with completely different internals. Software can't tell the difference by correctness, only by performance.
And as a designer, I think of the choices through the iron law: execution time is instruction count times CPI times clock period.
Pipelining and process technology attack the clock period, wide issue, caches and prediction attack the CPI, and the ISA and compiler mostly affect the instruction count.
Which choices you make depends on the target: a battery-powered sensor wants minimal area and energy per instruction, a server wants maximum single-thread and total throughput."
